chapter: Europe 1933, New York Cotton Club, Hodges group
title: Rose of the Rio Grande as a specialty and non-Ellington repertoire
summary: It became a specialty when recorded, and the book at first included popular tunes, later nearly all Ellington.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: And "Rose of the Rio Grande" you recorded in I think 1938 according to this discography. And
I read that it -- when did you start playing (14) -- do you remember?
No.
Much before --
You mean in the band?
Uh-huh.
With this band?
Uh-huh. Oh, was it a solo photo of yours?

No. I -- you know -- any tune we'd ever played I knew it, or knew most of it. So I never played a solo on it. You know, just like you'd go to play a dance, you'd play "Rose of the Rio Grande" or play any tune -- I had played it before with other little gig bands we called them.
But that's the first time it had been done as a sort of a specialty number.
Was when it was recorded.
Yes, when we recorded it.
You had not -- it had not been your solo --
No, no.
But the band -- it had it in the book.
Right.
Did the band have a lot of non-Ellington compositions in the book at that time, (inaudible)
(Simultaneous conversation)
Quite a few, yes. CAuse we played --
like when you play dances you can't play the same things all night you know. You make arrangements on popular tunes. You had to mix them in.
But later on the band book became almost exclusively Ellington, didn't it?

Well, as the years or times went by, the tunes that the public -- they came to know -- well the number became larger so pretty soon you played a whole night and not play anybody's tune but Ellington's -- or the Ellington named --
And they came to a point where he began deliberately adding other material -- pop other materials of -- but still the majority of the book stayed Ellington.
Right. Right, yeah. Uh-huh.
